source_text: Talem fuisse credendum est illum Iohannem monachum, quem de belli ciuilis euentu maior Theodosius consuluit imperator: habebat quippe etiam prophetiam. neque enim singulos singula munerum istorum, sed etiam plura unum habere posse non ambigo. Iohannes ergo iste cuidam mulieri religiosissimae inpatienter eum uidere cupienti atque ut hoc inpetraret per maritum suum uehementer instanti, cum ille nollet, quoniam id numquam permiserat feminis, uade, inquit, dic uxori tuae, uidebit me nocte proxima, sed in somnis. et factum est: monuitque illam quidquid fidelem coniugatam moneri oportebat. quae cum euigilasset, talem se uidisse hominem dei uiro suo, qualem ille eum nouerat, et quid ab illo audierit, iudicauit. qui hoc ab eis conperit, retulit mihi, uir grauis et nobilis et dignissimus credi. sed si illum sanctum monachum ipse uidissem, quia, sicut fertur, patientissime interrogabatur et sapientissime respondebat, quaesissem ab eo, quod ad istam pertinet quaestionem, utrum ipse ad illam feminam uenisset in somnis, id est spiritus eius in effigie corporis sui, sicut nos ipsos in effigie nostri corporis somniamus, an ipso aliud agente uel, si dormiebat, aliud somniante siue per angelum siue quocumque alio modo in mulieris somnio talis facta sit uisio, atque id futurum, ut ipse promitteret, prophetiae spiritu reuelante praesciuerit. si enim ipse interfuit somnianti, mirabili gratia utique id potuit, non natura, et dei munere, non propria facultate; si autem ipso aliud agente, siue dormiente et uisis aliis occupato, cum mulier uidit in somnis, profecto tale aliquid factum est, quale illud est, quod in apostolorum Actibus legimus, ubi dominus Iesus loquitur Ananiae de Saulo et indicat ei, quod Saulus uidit ad se uenientem Ananiam, cum hoc Ananias ipse nesciret. quodlibet horum mihi responderet ille homo dei, et de martyribus ab illo pergerem quaerere, utrum ipsi adsint in somnis uel quocumque alio modo uidentibus eos in qua figura uoluerint, et maxime quando ab eis se torqueri daemones in hominibus confitentur et rogant eos, ut pareant sibi, an ista fiant dei nutu per angelicas potestates in honorem commendationemque sanctorum ad utilitatem hominum illis in summa quiete positis et ad alia longe meliora uisa uacantibus seorsum a nobis orantibusque pro nobis; nam Mediolani apud sanctos Protasium et Geruasium martyres expresso nomine sicut defunctorum, quos eodem modo commemorabant, adhuc uiuum daemones episcopum confitebantur Ambrosium atque ut sibi parceret obsecrabant illo aliud agente atque hoc cum ageretur omnino nesciente; an uero aliquando per ipsam praesentiam martyrum fiant ista, aliquando per angelorum; et utrum possint uel quibus signis possint a nobis duo ista discerni, an ea sentire ac diiudicare non ualeat, nisi qui habeat illud donum per dei spiritum diuidentem propria unicuique prout uult: dissereret mihi, ut arbitror, ille Iohannes haec omnia, sicut uellem, ut aut eo docente discerem et ea quae audirem uera et certa esse cognoscerem, aut ego crederem quae nescirem illo dicente quae sciret. quodsi mihi forsitan de sancta scriptura responderet ac diceret: altiora te ne quaesieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris, sed quae tibi praecepit dominus, illa cogita semper, id etiam gratanter acciperem. non enim paruus est fructus, si aliqua obscura et incerta, quae conprehendere non ualemus, clarum saltem certumque sit nobis non esse quaerenda, et quod unusquisque uult discere putans prodesse si sciat, discat non obesse, si nesciat.
thought_title: John the monk's vision and the limits of knowing how the dead appear
orientation: Augustine is recounting a story about John the monk, a prophet consulted by the emperor Theodosius, and using it to raise questions about how visions of the dead or martyrs occur.
pass_a_gloss: Such a man must be believed to have been that John the monk, whom the elder Theodosius the emperor consulted about the outcome of the civil war: he had indeed also prophecy. For I do not doubt that individuals can have not single gifts of these, one each, but also several, one person. This John, then, to a certain most religious woman who was impatiently desiring to see him and who was pressing insistently through her husband that she might obtain this, when he was unwilling, because he had never permitted this to women, said: Go, tell your wife, she will see me next night, but in dreams. And it happened: and he advised her whatever a faithful married woman ought to be advised. When she had woken, she judged that she had seen such a man of God to her husband, as he knew him, and what she had heard from him. He who learned this from them reported it to me, a serious and noble man and most worthy to be believed. But if I myself had seen that holy monk, because, as is reported, he was questioned most patiently and answered most wisely, I would have asked him what pertains to this question, whether he himself had come to that woman in dreams, that is his spirit in the likeness of his body, just as we dream ourselves in the likeness of our body, or whether, while he himself was doing something else or, if he was sleeping, dreaming something else, such a vision was made in the woman's dream either through an angel or in some other way, and he foreknew by the revealing spirit of prophecy that it would happen, so that he promised it. For if he himself was present to the dreaming woman, he could do this by wonderful grace, not by nature, and by God's gift, not by his own ability; but if, while he himself was doing something else, or sleeping and occupied with other visions, the woman saw in dreams, then certainly something of such a kind happened as that which we read in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Lord Jesus speaks to Ananias about Saul and indicates to him that Saul saw Ananias coming to him, when Ananias himself did not know this. Whichever of these that man of God would answer me, I would also proceed to ask him about the martyrs, whether they themselves are present in dreams or in some other way to those seeing them in whatever form they wish, and especially when demons in people confess that they are tormented by them and ask them to spare them, whether these things happen by God's command through angelic powers for the honor and prayerful commending of the saints for the benefit of humans, while those saints are placed in the highest rest and are free for other far better sights, apart from us, and praying for us; for at Milan at the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, by express name just as of the dead whom they were commemorating in the same way, the demons confessed the still living bishop Ambrose and begged him to spare them, while he was doing something else and was entirely unaware when this was happening; or whether sometimes these things happen through the very presence of the martyrs, sometimes through angels; and whether they can be, or by what signs they can be, distinguished by us, these two things, or whether no one can perceive and judge these things unless he has that gift through the spirit of God dividing to each his own as he wills: that John, I think, would discuss all these things for me, as I would wish, so that either I would learn with him teaching and would recognize that the things I heard were true and certain, or I would believe what I did not know, with him saying what he knew. But if perhaps he should answer me from holy scripture and say: Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger than you, but what the Lord commanded you, think on those things always, I would also receive this gratefully. For it is not a small fruit, if some obscure and uncertain things, which we cannot grasp, are at least clear and certain to us that they are not to be sought, and that what each person wants to learn thinking it profits if he knows, he should learn that it does not harm if he does not know.

lemmas.gloss: being free for, having leisure for

choices.english: in the likeness of his body
choices.why: The glossary defines similitudo as 'likeness'; effigies is a near-synonym here for the dream-image of a person, and 'likeness' preserves the distinction from the actual body.
rejected: in the image of his body
in the form of his body

choices.why: The glossary requires 'prayerful commending' for commendatio, and the genitive sanctorum is objective: the saints are being commended, not doing the commending.
Summa quiete is ablative of place where; 'highest rest' keeps the superlative force and the spatial metaphor of positis.

choices.english: Do not seek things higher than you
choices.why: This is a scriptural allusion (Sirach 3:21); the comparative altiora with te is a standard construction meaning 'things too high for you', and the literal rendering preserves the biblical tone.
rejected: Do not seek what is too high for you

choices.english: dividing to each his own as he wills
choices.why: This echoes 1 Corinthians 12:11; 'dividing to each his own' keeps the distributive force of propria unicuique and the present participle.
rejected: apportioning to each one as he wills
distributing to each as he wills

pass_b_english: We must believe this was the kind of man John the monk was, the one the elder Emperor Theodosius consulted about the outcome of a civil war; for he also had the gift of prophecy. I have no doubt that one person can possess not just one of these gifts but several. This John, then, was sought by a very devout woman who was impatient to see him and pressed her husband insistently to obtain it for her. John refused, since he had never allowed women to visit him, but he said, "Go and tell your wife: she will see me next night, but in a dream." And so it happened. He gave her whatever counsel a faithful married woman needed to receive. When she woke, she told her husband that she had seen the man of God just as her husband knew him, and she reported what she had heard from him. The man who learned this from them told it to me—a serious and noble man, entirely worthy of belief.

But if I had seen that holy monk myself, since he is said to have answered questions with the greatest patience and wisdom, I would have asked him about the point relevant to this question: whether he himself had come to that woman in her dream—that is, whether his spirit had come in the likeness of his body, just as we dream of ourselves in the likeness of our body—or whether, while he was doing something else, or if he was asleep, dreaming something else, the vision was produced in the woman's dream through an angel or in some other way, and he foreknew that it would happen because the spirit of prophecy revealed it to him when he made the promise. For if he was actually present to her as she dreamed, he could do that only by a wonderful grace, not by nature—by God's gift, not by his own power. But if he was doing something else, or sleeping and occupied with other dreams, while the woman saw him in her dream, then something happened like what we read in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Lord Jesus speaks to Ananias about Saul and tells him that Saul has seen Ananias coming to him, though Ananias himself did not know it (Acts 9:12).

Whichever of these that man of God might answer me, I would go on to ask him about the martyrs: whether they themselves are present in dreams, or in whatever other way they appear to those who see them, in whatever form they wish—and especially when demons in people confess that they are being tormented by them and beg them to spare them. Are these things done by God's command through angelic powers, for the honor and prayerful commending of the saints and for the benefit of human beings, while the saints themselves are placed in the highest rest and are free for other, far better visions, apart from us and praying for us? For at Milan, at the shrines of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, demons called by name not only the dead whom they were commemorating in the same way but also Ambrose, the bishop, who was still alive, and begged him to spare them—while Ambrose was doing something else and had no idea this was happening. Or are these things sometimes done through the actual presence of the martyrs, and sometimes through angels? And can the two be distinguished by us, and by what signs—or can no one perceive and judge these things except the one who has that gift through God's Spirit, who divides to each his own as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11)?

I believe John would have discussed all these things with me as I wished, so that either I would learn from his teaching and recognize that what I heard was true and certain, or I would believe what I did not know because he was telling me what he knew. But if he had perhaps answered me from holy Scripture and said, "Do not seek things too high for you, and do not search out things too strong for you; but think always on what the Lord has commanded you" (Sirach 3:21-22), I would have accepted that too with gratitude. For it is no small fruit if, when some obscure and uncertain matters are beyond our grasp, it becomes at least clear and certain to us that they should not be sought after—and that whatever anyone wants to learn, thinking it will help him to know it, he should learn that it does him no harm not to know it.

problems.quote: whether they themselves are present in dreams, or in whatever other way they appear to those who see them, in whatever form they choose
problems.source_quote: utrum ipsi adsint in somnis uel quocumque alio modo uidentibus eos in qua figura uoluerint
problems.why: 'in qua figura uoluerint' likely means 'in whatever form they (the viewers) wish,' not 'they choose' — ambiguous but 'choose' assigns agency to martyrs.
problems.ruling: 'voluerint' subject is 'ipsi' (martyrs), but 'videntibus eos' (viewers) intervenes; 'choose' misleads on agency. Ambiguous Latin, but 'they wish' = viewers is more natural reading.

problems.quote: Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger than you
problems.source_quote: altiora te ne quaesieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris
problems.why: Wrong comparative sense: 'altiora' = 'too high for you', 'fortiora' = 'too strong for you'—the English 'higher than you' and 'stronger than you' suggests comparison of persons, not capacity. 'Things too high for you' and 'things too strong for you' or 'beyond your strength'.
problems.fix: Do not seek things too high for you, and do not search out things too strong for you
problems.ruling: 'higher than you' and 'stronger than you' misrender 'altiora te/fortiora te' = 'things too high/strong for you'; Sirach 3:21-22 means beyond one's capacity.

edits.old: Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger than you
edits.new: Do not seek things too high for you, and do not search out things too strong for you

fixed: Changed 'they choose' to 'they wish' to remove the implication that the martyrs choose the form; the Latin 'uoluerint' is ambiguous but the context suggests the viewers' wish.
Changed 'higher than you' and 'stronger than you' to 'too high for you' and 'too strong for you' to reflect the comparative sense of 'altiora te' and 'fortiora te' as exceeding one's capacity.

last_rejected.quote: the shrines of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius
last_rejected.source_quote: apud sanctos Protasium et Geruasium martyres
last_rejected.why: Source says 'at/with the holy martyrs P and G,' not 'at the shrines of.' Augustine means at their memorial shrines, but the English adds 'shrines of' not in source.
last_rejected.fix: at the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius
last_rejected.ruling: 'apud sanctos martyres' in context of cult and demons confessing means at their shrines/memorials; 'shrines' is implied sense, not misleading.

last_rejected.source_quote: Iohannes ergo iste cuidam mulieri religiosissimae inpatienter eum uidere cupienti atque ut hoc inpetraret per maritum suum uehementer instanti, cum ille nollet
last_rejected.why: John refused the woman; she sought him, not vice versa. English inverts agency.
last_rejected.fix: This John, then—a certain very devout woman, impatient to see him, pressed her husband insistently to obtain it for her, but he refused
last_rejected.ruling: 'Iohannes ergo iste cuidam mulieri...inpatienter eum uidere cupienti' = John was sought by woman eager to see him. Agency is correct.

last_rejected.quote: John refused, since he had never allowed women to visit him
last_rejected.source_quote: cum ille nollet, quoniam id numquam permiserat feminis
last_rejected.why: Subject of 'nollet' and 'permiserat' is John, not the husband; John never permitted women.
last_rejected.fix: when he [John] refused, since he had never permitted women
last_rejected.ruling: 'cum ille nollet, quoniam id numquam permiserat feminis' = John refused, since he never permitted women. Translation is correct.

last_rejected.quote: Go and tell your wife: she will see me next night, but in a dream
last_rejected.source_quote: uade, inquit, dic uxori tuae, uidebit me nocte proxima, sed in somnis
last_rejected.why: Speaker is John addressing the husband, not 'he said' ambiguously; 'inquit' marks direct speech.
last_rejected.fix: he said, 'Go, tell your wife: she will see me next night, but in a dream'
last_rejected.ruling: 'uade, inquit, dic uxori tuae' = 'Go, he said, tell your wife.' English correctly renders John addressing the husband in direct speech.

last_rejected.quote: He gave her whatever counsel a faithful married woman needed to receive
last_rejected.source_quote: monuitque illam quidquid fidelem coniugatam moneri oportebat
last_rejected.why: 'monuit' means warned/admonished, not counsel; 'coniugatam' is married woman, but sense is warning.
last_rejected.fix: and warned her of whatever a faithful married woman needed to be warned about
last_rejected.ruling: 'monuit' ranges from warn to admonish to counsel; 'counsel' is acceptable. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: just as her husband knew him
last_rejected.why: 'ille' refers to the husband, but 'nouerat' means knew of/recognized, not personal acquaintance.
last_rejected.fix: such as her husband knew him to be
last_rejected.ruling: 'nouerat' means 'knew'; 'just as her husband knew him' is within normal range. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the point relevant to this question
last_rejected.why: 'istam' is 'this' (the present question being discussed), not 'the point relevant'.
last_rejected.fix: what pertains to this very question
last_rejected.ruling: 'quod ad istam pertinet quaestionem' = 'what pertains to this question.' 'The point relevant to this question' is acceptable rendering.

last_rejected.quote: whether he himself had come to that woman in her dream—that is, whether his spirit had come in the likeness of his body
last_rejected.source_quote: utrum ipse ad illam feminam uenisset in somnis, id est spiritus eius in effigie corporis sui
last_rejected.why: 'in somnis' is 'in dreams' (dative/ablative plural), not 'in her dream'; 'effigie' is image/form, not likeness.
last_rejected.fix: whether he himself had come to that woman in dreams, that is, his spirit in the image of his body
last_rejected.ruling: 'in somnis' = 'in dreams'; 'effigie' = 'likeness/form.' Both renderings are within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: while he was doing something else, or if he was asleep, dreaming something else
last_rejected.source_quote: ipso aliud agente uel, si dormiebat, aliud somniante
last_rejected.why: English adds 'if' making conditional what is participial; 'dormiebat' is indicative, part of the participial construction.
last_rejected.fix: while he was doing something else or, if he was sleeping, dreaming something else
last_rejected.ruling: 'si dormiebat' is itself conditional; English 'or if he was asleep' faithfully renders the Latin. Not an error.

last_rejected.quote: the vision was produced in the woman's dream
last_rejected.source_quote: in mulieris somnio talis facta sit uisio
last_rejected.why: English adds 'produced' and 'dream' singular; 'somnio' is dative/ablative, 'in the woman's dream-vision'.
last_rejected.fix: such a vision was made in the woman's dream
last_rejected.ruling: 'in mulieris somnio...facta sit uisio' = 'the vision was produced/made in the woman's dream.' Acceptable rendering.

last_rejected.quote: because the spirit of prophecy revealed it to him when he made the promise
last_rejected.source_quote: atque id futurum, ut ipse promitteret, prophetiae spiritu reuelante praesciuerit
last_rejected.why: 'ut ipse promitteret' is 'as he himself promised', not 'when he made the promise'; 'praesciuerit' is foreknew.
last_rejected.fix: and that it would happen, as he himself promised, he foreknew by the spirit of prophecy revealing it
last_rejected.ruling: 'ut ipse promitteret' can mean 'when he promised'; 'praesciuerit' = 'foreknew.' Translation conveys meaning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: while the saints themselves are placed in the highest rest
last_rejected.why: 'positis' is ablative absolute, 'while they are placed/resting', not passive 'are placed'.
last_rejected.fix: while they themselves are resting in the highest quiet
last_rejected.ruling: 'in summa quiete positis' = 'placed in highest rest.' Passive 'are placed' is acceptable for ablative absolute.

last_rejected.quote: demons called by name not only the dead whom they were commemorating in the same way but also Ambrose
last_rejected.source_quote: daemones expresso nomine sicut defunctorum, quos eodem modo commemorabant, adhuc uiuum daemones episcopum confitebantur Ambrosium
last_rejected.why: English garbles syntax: demons confessed by name, as they did of the dead, also the living Ambrose.
last_rejected.fix: demons confessed by name, as they did of the dead whom they were commemorating in the same way, also Ambrose the bishop, still living
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly states demons called by name the dead and also living Ambrose. Syntax is accurately rendered.
